answers.answer: SCOPe 2.08 places NAD(P)-binding enzymes in several unrelated folds and even in different classes, so NAD(P) binding has arisen more than once. Within a single superfamily such as the NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domains (c.2.1, fold c.2, sunid 51735) the diversity of families (alcohol dehydrogenase-like c.2.1.1, tyrosine-dependent oxidoreductases c.2.1.2, GAPDH N-terminal c.2.1.3, LDH N-terminal-like c.2.1.5, 6-phosphogluconate DH c.2.1.6, Rex repressor c.2.1.12, etc.) is divergent evolution: SCOP's superfamily level asserts probable common ancestry based on shared structure plus shared functional features (the GxGxxG dinucleotide-binding motif, the same cofactor position at the C-terminal edge of the parallel sheet with the pyrophosphate over the first beta-alpha-beta crossover). The family level adds clear sequence similarity. By contrast, NAD(P) binding ALSO occurs in the FAD/NAD(P)-binding domain fold c.3 (superfamily c.3.1, sunid 51905; a b/b/a 3-layer fold with a 5-stranded parallel sheet order 32145 plus an antiparallel meander), the Nucleotide-binding domain fold c.4 (c.4.1; a/b/a, order 32145, 'Rossmann-like'), the DHS-like NAD/FAD-binding fold c.31 (c.31.1, sunid 52467; order 321456, containing deoxyhypusine synthase, transhydrogenase dIII and the Sir2 family c.31.1.5), the ALDH-like fold c.82 (aldehyde dehydrogenases, which bind NAD in a non-classical mode), and outside class c entirely in the a+b class, e.g. the NAD-binding domain of HMG-CoA reductase (d.58.20, sunid 55035) under the Ferredoxin-like fold d.58 and the FwdE/GAPDH domain-like fold d.81. Because these are separate folds, SCOP makes no claim of common ancestry between them; the fold level is a purely topological grouping. SCOPe's own curator comment on fold c.2 (sunid 51734) says only that 'the nucleotide-binding modes of this and the next two folds/superfamilies are similar', explicitly describing similar binding modes without merging the folds, i.e. the curators treat c.2, c.3 and c.4 as plausibly convergent or at best unresolved. The implication is that the capacity to bind a ubiquitous, ancient cofactor like NAD(P) is a strong functional constraint that independent lineages can satisfy with different scaffolds (convergence), while within each superfamily the many enzymes with different substrates and chemistries (dehydrogenases, reductases, transcription factors, channel domains) illustrate divergence from one ancestral cofactor-binding domain. Cofactor binding or active-site similarity alone is insufficient evidence of homology because (1) ligand-driven convergence is well documented: the same adenine-dinucleotide pocket geometry can be built by different topologies, and the glycine-rich loop is a short, low-complexity motif that is easily reinvented; (2) SCOP homology inference at superfamily level requires a combination of independent lines of evidence (shared core topology and architecture, structural conservation of regions beyond the active site, conserved sequence motifs in equivalent structural positions, conserved unusual features such as domain organisation or metal/ligand sites) and ideally detectable sequence similarity (e.g. HMM or PSI-BLAST hits, or statistically significant structural alignments such as FATCAT/DALI covering the whole core); (3) a shared fold alone is not homology either (many a/b doubly wound Rossmann-like folds are thought to arise independently), so the shared Rossmann-like strand order 321456 between c.2 and c.31 is no proof of common ancestry; and (4) function is not a reliable phylogenetic marker: within c.2.1 the Rex repressor and the potassium channel NAD-binding domain (c.2.1.9) have lost catalytic function, whereas enzymes in different folds carry out the same NAD-dependent chemistry. Practical limits: do not transfer function or catalytic mechanism between NAD(P)-binding domains merely because both bind NAD(P); do not use a c.2.1 structure as a homology-modelling template for a c.3.1, c.31.1, c.82 or d.58.20 protein; and when a new protein is detected only by an active-site or cofactor-motif match, independent evidence (significant sequence-profile similarity, whole-domain structural superposition, conserved motif positions in equivalent secondary structure elements, and ideally phylogenetic continuity through intermediate sequences) is required before assigning it to a SCOPe superfamily. Family-level (clear sequence) and superfamily-level (probable common ancestry) assignments are evolutionary claims; fold-level and class-level groupings are not.
